title: MOSES LIFTED HIS STAFF—AND THE SEA SPLIT OPEN
paragraphs:
MOSES LIFTED HIS STAFF—AND THE SEA SPLIT OPEN
They thought they were trapped between Pharaoh and the water. But sometimes the place that looks like your grave becomes the road God uses to lead you into freedom.
Imagine hearing the chariots before you can clearly see them.
Not one.
Hundreds.
The pounding of horses.
The grinding of wheels.
The shouting of soldiers.
Children crying.
Mothers clutching them tighter.
Men looking desperately for somewhere—anywhere—to run.
And directly in front of them...
water.
Behind them stood the empire they had just escaped.
Before them stretched a sea they could not cross.
And somewhere in that terrified crowd, somebody must have thought:
“We should never have left.”
That is one of the most frightening things fear can do.
It can make slavery look safer than freedom.
It can make yesterday's chains seem preferable to tomorrow's uncertainty.
It can make you question the very deliverance you once prayed for.
Maybe that is why this story has survived thousands of years and still reaches into the human heart.
Because Egypt changes names.
Pharaoh changes faces.
But we still know what it feels like to stand between something we cannot defeat and something we cannot cross.
Maybe your “Egypt” was an addiction you promised Jesus you would never return to.
Maybe it was pornography.
Alcohol.
Bitterness.
A relationship you knew was destroying your walk with God.
Secret sin.
An old identity.
A season of shame nobody at church knows about.
Maybe you finally walked away...
and then discovered that leaving Egypt does not mean Egypt immediately stops chasing you.
That is where Exodus 14 becomes painfully personal.
Israel had been delivered, but Pharaoh pursued them.
They were free...
but they did not yet feel safe.
And when they saw Pharaoh's army approaching, they panicked.
They cried to Moses in bitter fear, essentially asking why he had brought them into the wilderness to die.
Then Moses spoke words believers have repeated through generations:
“The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace.”
But what happens next is fascinating.
God tells Moses:
“Wherefore criest thou unto me? speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward.”
Go forward?
There was a sea forward.
Yet God said...
forward.
Then came the command recorded in Exodus 14:16:
“וְאַתָּ֞ה הָרֵ֣ם אֶת־מַטְּךָ֗ וּנְטֵ֧ה אֶת־יָדְךָ֛ עַל־הַיָּ֖ם וּבְקָעֵ֑הוּ”
Ve'attah harem et-mattecha, uneteh et-yadcha al-hayyam uveqa'ehu...
In context:
“You, lift up your staff, stretch out your hand over the sea, and divide it.”
The Hebrew is powerful.
Matteh—מַטֶּה—is the staff or rod.
Yad—יָד—is the hand.
Yam—יָם—is the sea.
And uveqa'ehu comes from the Hebrew root בקע, carrying the idea of splitting, cleaving, or breaking open.
But don't miss what Scripture is actually saying.
The staff was not magical.
Moses was not the source of supernatural power.
This is not a story about a powerful man discovering the secret ability hidden inside himself.
The Bible gives the glory somewhere else.
Exodus 14:21 says:
“וַיֵּט מֹשֶׁה אֶת־יָדוֹ עַל־הַיָּם”
Moses stretched out his hand over the sea.
And then...
“וַיּוֹלֶךְ יְהוָה אֶת־הַיָּם”
YHWH drove the sea back.
That changes everything.
Moses stretched out his hand.
God made the way.
Moses obeyed.
God displayed the power.
Moses lifted what was in his hand.
God moved what no human hand could move.
And perhaps somebody reading this desperately needs that distinction.
You are not God.
You do not have to be.
You cannot split every sea.
You cannot control every outcome.
You cannot force your prodigal child home.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot make another person repent.
You cannot resurrect a dead relationship by sheer determination.
You cannot heal every wound by pretending it doesn't hurt.
You cannot defeat sin through self-confidence.
You cannot save yourself.
But you can obey the God who can do what you cannot.
There are moments when faith looks less like understanding everything and more like taking the next obedient step while the sea is still in front of you.
Think about Israel standing there.
God had not merely rescued them from inconvenience.
He had brought slaves out of Egypt.
Generations had lived beneath Pharaoh's system.
Egypt had shaped their routines, their fears, their expectations.
Then God intervened.
The Passover had come.
Blood had marked the doors.
Judgment passed over those sheltered according to God's provision.
Israel walked out.
And now Pharaoh wanted them back.
There is something hauntingly familiar about that.
Because sometimes after Jesus begins changing your life, the old master comes looking for you.
The temptation returns.
The memories return.
The craving returns.
The shame whispers again.
The old friends call.
The old anger wakes up.
The old version of you seems to say:
“You really thought you escaped me?”
And suddenly you are standing at your own Red Sea wondering whether anything actually changed.
Listen carefully.
The presence of pursuit does not mean the absence of deliverance.
Israel could hear Pharaoh behind them while God was still leading them.
That means your battle is not automatically evidence that God abandoned you.
Temptation does not prove your repentance was fake.
A difficult road does not prove you chose the wrong Savior.
Sometimes freedom has a wilderness attached to it.
Sometimes obedience takes you somewhere you could never survive without God.
And that is exactly where human pride begins to die.
Because Israel could not boast afterward:
“We defeated Egypt.”
They didn't.
They could not say:
“We engineered a bridge.”
They didn't.
They could not say:
“We were simply stronger than Pharaoh.”
They weren't.
Their situation was deliberately beyond their ability.
Then God acted.
The text says YHWH drove the sea back with a strong east wind through the night and made the sea dry ground.
The waters divided.
Imagine being there.
Not reading it safely from your phone.
Standing there.
Wind screaming across the water.
Darkness around you.
The pillar of God's presence separating Israel from the Egyptians.
And slowly...
the impossible begins opening.
Where there had been water, there is now a road.
Where there had been certain death, there is passage.
Where fear had screamed, “This is where your story ends,” God creates a path nobody in the crowd could have manufactured.
Then comes the terrifying part.
They have to walk through it.
Imagine taking that first step.
Water beside you.
Water on the other side.
Your children beside you.
Egypt behind you.
The only direction left is through.
Faith is beautiful when printed on coffee mugs.
It is much harder when your feet have to move.
Yet Israel went into the midst of the sea on dry ground.
They walked.
One frightened step after another.
And the same place that became Israel's road to freedom became the place where Pharaoh's pursuing forces were overwhelmed.
Don't turn that into a promise that God will destroy everyone who hurts you.
The biblical point is greater than personal revenge.
YHWH was revealing His glory, judging Egypt's oppression, keeping His covenant purposes, and showing both Israel and Egypt who truly was Lord.
God was not merely making Moses impressive.
God was making His own name known.
And that is why the story should never become “Believe in yourself and your sea will split.”
That is far too small.
Exodus is not self-help.
It is revelation.
The hero is God.
And the Gospel takes that truth even deeper.
Because the greatest bondage humanity faces is not Pharaoh.
It is sin.
Our greatest problem is not simply that bad things happened to us.
Scripture says something much more uncomfortable.
We have sinned.
We have rebelled.
We have loved darkness.
We have carried guilt we cannot wash away ourselves.
We do not merely need better circumstances.
We need reconciliation with God.
And this is where the road from scandal to grace becomes breathtaking.
At the Red Sea, God made a way where Israel could not make one.
At the cross, God provided the way sinners could never provide for themselves.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to inspire enslaved people to try harder.
He came to save.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And He rose again.
The Gospel does not tell you to lift your own moral staff high enough until the sea of judgment finally moves.
The Gospel tells you that salvation is found in Jesus Christ.
Grace is not God pretending sin doesn't matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin matters so terribly that the Son of God suffered and died.
Yet love reaches so deeply that Christ willingly gave Himself for sinners.
That means the ugliest chapter of your life does not have to become the final chapter.
The affair.
The addiction.
The lie.
The years you wasted.
The secret browser history.
The bitterness you fed.
The marriage you damaged.
The child you failed.
The faith you abandoned.
The church mask you wore while privately collapsing.
None of those things should be minimized.
Sin must be called sin.
Repentance matters.
Truth matters.
But shame does not get to rewrite the Gospel.
Jesus does.
That is the scandal of grace.
Christ receives sinners who come to Him.
Not because rebellion is insignificant...
but because His mercy is greater than the sinner's ability to rescue himself.
Maybe your sea has not opened yet.
Maybe that is the sentence that caught you.
You have prayed.
Waited.
Cried.
Obeyed as best you know how.
And the water is still there.
Please do not turn Exodus 14 into a formula promising that every earthly obstacle will miraculously disappear if you possess enough faith.
The Bible does not give us that promise.
Some seas open.
Some thorns remain.
Some believers are delivered from danger.
Others glorify Christ through suffering and even death.
The ultimate Christian hope is not that every circumstance becomes comfortable.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
He is faithful in deliverance.
Faithful in suffering.
Faithful in life.
Faithful in death.
And because He rose, everyone who belongs to Him has a future beyond the grave.
So perhaps the question tonight is not merely:
“When will God split my sea?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
“Will I trust Him when I cannot yet see the road?”
Because Israel saw water before they saw dry ground.
Moses heard God's command before he saw God's intervention.
Obedience came before the visible pathway.
And somewhere between Egypt and freedom, a generation learned something they desperately needed to know:
Pharaoh was not God.
The sea was not God.
Moses was not God.
The staff was not God.
YHWH is God.
And Christian, the One who ultimately reveals the Father to us is Jesus Christ.
So stop worshiping the obstacle.
Stop measuring God's power by the size of what frightens you.
Stop letting yesterday's Pharaoh convince you that you still belong to him.
If you are in Christ, your sin no longer owns the final word.
Your shame does not own the final word.
Your past does not own the final word.
Jesus does.
Maybe you stumbled again.
Come back.
Maybe you've been hiding.
Step into the light.
Maybe your prayers have become cold.
Call upon Him again.
Maybe everybody thinks you're strong while privately you are exhausted.
Tell the truth.
Maybe you have never genuinely surrendered your life to Jesus Christ at all.
Then don't merely admire Moses.
Don't merely admire miracles.
Come to Christ.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
The greatest miracle you need is not water moving out of your way.
You need a heart reconciled to God.
And Jesus Christ is still saving sinners.
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only person struggling to keep walking.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, don't dismiss that.
Not to embarrass them.
Not because you know everything they're going through.
But because sometimes one Scripture-centered reminder arrives on the exact night somebody was considering going back to Egypt.
There may come a night when the chariots sound louder than God's promises and you need to read Exodus 14 again.
Not as a religious performance.
Not as a bargain with God.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with Him—it does not.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and sharing biblical truth can be one simple expression of wanting others to hear about Him.
If this message strengthened you, sharing it may place the Gospel in front of someone Gospel Warrior could never reach otherwise.
That matters.
It does not buy salvation.
It does not make God love you more.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.

But supporting Gospel-centered work can be a practical act of generosity that helps biblical content keep reaching people who are hurting, questioning, searching, repenting, and trying to grow deeper in Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend quietly drifting from church.
Invite the believer fighting an addiction.
Invite the person angry with God.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the person whose life looks completely put together but whose soul is exhausted.
Because somebody else's Pharaoh may be gaining ground tonight.
Somebody is standing at the water.
Somebody thinks their story is over.
Somebody thinks their past has finally caught them.
And maybe God will use the Scripture you share—not your perfection, not your eloquence, not your reputation—to remind them where salvation is found.
Moses lifted the staff.
Moses stretched out his hand.
But God split the sea.
Never confuse the instrument with the Savior.
The same God who made a road through impossible waters ultimately gave us something infinitely greater than a pathway through the sea.
He gave us His Son.
And when Jesus Christ walked out of the tomb, death itself learned what Pharaoh learned at the water:
God gets the final word.
So when your past comes thundering behind you and fear tells you there is nowhere left to go...
look to Christ.
Repent.
Trust Him.
And when He tells you to walk in obedience...
go forward.
Because sometimes what looks like the place where your story will drown becomes the very place where you discover whose hands have been holding your story all along.
The sea was never the greatest miracle. The greater wonder is that a holy God still makes a way for guilty people to come home—and that Way has a name: Jesus.
